name: Microservices
description: Service boundaries, communication, data ownership, and honest accounting of what distribution costs.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Microservices is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: Monolith vs microservices
cards.answer: A monolith is one application deployed as a single unit; a microservice architecture splits the system into many small services that are deployed independently and talk over the network.

left.title: Monolith
points: Simple to build, test and run

right.title: Microservices
points: Teams own and release services separately
Network calls — can fail or be slow
Scale each part separately, at high operational cost

cards.explanation: Most systems should start as a well-structured monolith. Microservices pay off when many teams need to ship independently; adopted too early, they add distributed-systems problems with none of the benefits.

cards.prompt: What is a microservice?
cards.answer: A small, independently deployable service that owns one business capability (orders, payments, notifications) along with its own data, and exposes it to other services through an API or messages.
cards.explanation: The defining property is independence: a team can change, deploy and scale its service without coordinating a release with everyone else.

cards.prompt: How do microservices communicate?
cards.answer: Synchronously, by calling each other's APIs (HTTP/REST or gRPC) and waiting for a reply; or asynchronously, by publishing events and messages to a broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ) that other services consume in their own time.
cards.explanation: Synchronous calls are simpler but chain failures together; asynchronous messaging decouples services but makes flows harder to follow and debug.

cards.prompt: Why does each microservice usually own its own database?
cards.answer: So services stay independent: if two services share tables, neither can change its schema without breaking the other, and they must be deployed together — losing the main benefit of microservices.
cards.explanation: The cost is that data spans services: no cross-service joins or transactions, so you use APIs, events and eventual consistency instead.

cards.prompt: What is an API gateway?
cards.answer: A single entry point that sits in front of many backend services and routes each client request to the right one, often also handling authentication, rate limiting, TLS and response aggregation.
cards.explanation: Clients get one stable address instead of knowing about dozens of internal services, and cross-cutting concerns are handled once instead of in every service.

modules.name: Boundaries & Ownership
modules.description: Where to cut, who owns what data, and when not to split at all.

cards.prompt: A five-person team wants to split their app into twelve microservices. What do you say?
cards.answer: Don't. Start with a well-modularised monolith. Microservices solve organisational scaling — independent deploy cadence across many teams — and they cost you distributed transactions, network failure, versioning, and twelve pipelines to maintain.
cards.explanation: Conway's Law is the real driver: service boundaries end up mirroring team boundaries. With one team you get all the distribution costs and none of the independence benefit. Extract a service when a module has a genuinely different scaling, deploy or ownership profile.

cards.prompt: What is a bounded context, and why is it the right unit for a service?
cards.answer: A boundary within which a domain model and its language are consistent. 'Customer' means something different in billing, support and shipping — a bounded context lets each keep its own model instead of forcing one bloated shared one.
cards.explanation: Boundaries drawn by technical layer (a 'database service') produce chatty, coupled services. Boundaries drawn by business capability produce services that can change independently — which was the entire point of splitting.

cards.prompt: What is wrong with this architecture?
cards.code:
orders-service   ─┐
payments-service ─┼──►  shared_production_db  (all services read/write all tables)
users-service    ─┘
cards.answer: A shared database is a shared, invisible contract. No service can change its schema without breaking others, and you have a distributed monolith — all the deployment coupling, plus network calls.
cards.explanation: Database-per-service is the rule: each owns its data and exposes it only through its API or events. The cost is that joins across services become API calls or read models, which is exactly the trade-off you accepted when you split.

cards.prompt: Modular monolith vs microservices
cards.answer: Both enforce boundaries; only microservices pay the network to do it.

left.title: Modular monolith
points: One deploy, one place to debug
Boundaries enforced by discipline and tooling

right.title: Microservices
points: Independent deploy and scaling per service

cards.explanation: A modular monolith with clean module boundaries is the best preparation for extraction: when a module genuinely needs its own lifecycle, the seam already exists. Going the other way — merging distributed services — is much harder.

modules.name: Communication & Operations
modules.description: Sync vs async, gateways, service discovery and running a fleet.

cards.prompt: Synchronous request/response vs asynchronous events
cards.answer: Synchronous is simple and immediate but couples availability; asynchronous decouples but gives up immediate consistency.

left.title: Sync (REST/gRPC)
points: Immediate answer, easy to reason about
Caller is down if callee is down

cards.explanation: Use sync when the caller genuinely needs the answer to continue; async for notifications, fan-out and anything that can complete later. A chain of five synchronous calls multiplies failure probability and adds every hop's latency.

cards.prompt: What does an API gateway do?
cards.answer: It gives clients one entry point and handles cross-cutting concerns: routing, authentication, rate limiting, TLS termination, request aggregation and protocol translation.
cards.explanation: Without one, every client must know every service address and re-implement auth. The risk is the gateway becoming a monolith of business logic — keep it to cross-cutting concerns. The BFF pattern (a gateway per client type) avoids one gateway serving contradictory needs.

cards.prompt: When does a service mesh earn its complexity?
cards.answer: When you have enough services that mTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting and golden metrics should be uniform and out of application code — typically dozens of services across several teams and languages.
cards.explanation: A mesh moves those concerns into sidecars, so a Python service and a Go service behave identically. Below that scale, libraries and a gateway are simpler. The cost is real: extra hops, sidecar resources, and a new control plane to debug.

resources.title: Istio — What is a service mesh?

cards.prompt: How do you change a service's API without coordinating a big-bang deploy?
cards.answer: Make every change backwards compatible and deploy in two steps: add the new field or endpoint and support both, migrate consumers, then remove the old. Consumer-driven contract tests catch breakage before release.
cards.explanation: In a distributed system, old and new versions always run simultaneously — during rolling deploys if nothing else. Any change that requires services to deploy in a specific order has recreated the monolith's coupling without its safety.

cards.prompt: What is a distributed monolith, and how do you recognise one?
cards.answer: Services that must be deployed together, share a database, break when one changes, or require a specific release order. You pay every cost of distribution and get none of the independence.
cards.explanation: Diagnostic questions: can you deploy one service on a Friday without checking with anyone? Can it run when its neighbours are down? If either answer is no, the boundary is wrong — and merging back is a legitimate fix.

modules.name: Running Microservices
modules.description: Service discovery, migration with the strangler fig, cross-service queries, configuration, team topologies and independent deployability.

cards.prompt: How do services find each other when instances come and go constantly?
cards.answer: Through service discovery: instances register (or are registered by the platform) in a registry, and callers resolve a stable name to healthy instances. In Kubernetes, a Service gives a stable DNS name and virtual IP; elsewhere Consul, Eureka or cloud load balancers play the role.
cards.explanation: Client-side discovery lets callers pick instances and balance load themselves; server-side discovery puts a load balancer in between. Either way, health checks drive membership — a registry that keeps dead instances is worse than none.

cards.prompt: How do you migrate a large monolith to new services without a big-bang rewrite?
cards.answer: The strangler fig pattern: put a routing layer (proxy or gateway) in front of the monolith, then move one capability at a time into new code, routing its traffic there while everything else still goes to the monolith. The old system shrinks until it can be retired.
cards.explanation: Each step is small, reversible and delivers value. Big-bang rewrites famously fail because the old system keeps changing while the new one chases feature parity. Start with a capability that has clear boundaries and real reasons to move.

cards.prompt: The order history page needs data owned by the orders, customers and shipping services. How do you query across them?
cards.answer: Either API composition — a BFF or composer service calls each service and joins the results in memory (simple, but latency and availability depend on every call) — or a dedicated read model: a service builds its own denormalised view by subscribing to the other services' events, answering the query locally.
cards.explanation: This is the price of database-per-service: joins become integration. Use composition for low-volume screens, and event-fed read models (CQRS) for hot or complex queries. Never reach into another service's database directly.

cards.prompt: How should configuration be handled across many services and environments?
cards.answer: Keep configuration out of the build: the same artefact receives environment-specific settings at deploy time (environment variables, mounted files or a config service), with secrets from a secret manager. Validate configuration at startup and fail fast on anything missing or malformed.
cards.explanation: This is the twelve-factor principle of separating config from code. Centralised dynamic config and feature-flag services allow changes without redeploying — powerful, but treat config changes like code changes, with review, audit and rollback, because they cause many incidents.

cards.prompt: What are the four team types in Team Topologies, and how do they relate to service boundaries?
cards.answer: Stream-aligned teams own a flow of business value end to end; platform teams provide internal self-service products that reduce their load; enabling teams coach and upskill; complicated-subsystem teams own areas needing deep specialist knowledge. Interaction modes are collaboration, X-as-a-service, and facilitating.
cards.explanation: It operationalises Conway's law: design teams around the architecture you want and limit each team's cognitive load. Service boundaries that cut across team boundaries create constant coordination — the distributed-monolith symptom in organisational form.

cards.prompt: What has to be true for each service to be deployed independently, any day, without coordination?
cards.answer: Backwards-compatible APIs and events (additive changes, tolerant readers), consumer contract tests in each provider's pipeline, a separate pipeline per service, no shared database, feature flags to decouple release from deploy, and observability good enough to spot a bad deploy and roll it back quickly.
cards.explanation: Independent deployability is the whole point of microservices — if releases need a coordinated schedule, the costs of distribution are being paid for nothing. Track how often deployments require changes to other services as an architecture health metric.
